# Why Language Models Hallucinate: Deep Reference

**Source:** Adam Tauman Kalai, Ofir Nachum, Santosh S. Vempala, and Edwin Zhang, “Why Language Models Hallucinate”, arXiv:2509.04664v1, 4 September 2025. DOI: https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2509.04664.
**Scope:** open — CC BY 4.0.
**Source form:** Complete official arXiv TeX submission and BBL bibliography, checked against the 36-page official PDF. The clean citation anchors are the paper's numbered sections and appendices; the TeX conversion does not preserve reliable page boundaries.

**Structure:** Abstract; §1 Introduction (§1.1 pretraining errors; §1.2 post-training persistence); §2 Related work; §3 Pretraining Errors (§3.1 reduction without prompts; §3.2 reduction with prompts; §3.3 error factors, including §3.3.1 arbitrary facts and §3.3.2 poor models; §3.4 additional factors); §4 Post-training and hallucination (§4.1 evaluation incentives; §4.2 explicit confidence targets); §5 Discussion and limitations; §6 Conclusions; Appendix A proof of the main theorem; Appendix B arbitrary-facts analysis; Appendix C poor-model analysis; Appendix D computational hardness; Appendix E post-training proof; Appendix F current evaluation grading; 94-item bibliography.
**Citation style:** Numbered section and section title, or appendix letter and heading: `(§ N, "Section name")`, `(Appendix A–F, "Heading")`.
**Coverage:** full text and full image scope. All body sections, six appendices, footnotes, bibliography, and both numbered figures were read; the figures (Figure 1, and Figure 2's two panels) were visually inspected in the official PDF. No readable section was skipped, but the converted tape lacks one of the PDF's nine numbered footnotes (see Complete-source coverage).

---

## Authors' thesis

The paper gives a two-stage account of language-model hallucination. During pretraining, generative errors arise from familiar statistical sources of classification error: missing information about arbitrary facts, model-family or model-fit limitations, computational hardness, distribution shift, and erroneous training data. The authors formalise this by using a base language model as an **Is-It-Valid (IIV)** binary classifier and lower-bounding that model's generation error in terms of the induced classifier's error. During post-training, plausible falsehoods persist because influential binary evaluations reward guessing and give abstention no credit. The proposed mitigation is therefore socio-technical: modify mainstream benchmarks and leaderboards so that their instructions and scoring reward calibrated abstention, rather than merely adding specialised hallucination evaluations [AP] (§1, “Introduction”; §1.1, “Errors caused by pretraining”; §1.2, “Why hallucinations survive post-training”; §4, “Post-training and hallucination”).

The account is multi-factor: errors “may occur due to a combination of multiple factors” [V] (§3.4, “Additional factors”). The paper distinguishes multiple pretraining error factors, makes its central lower bounds under explicit assumptions, and characterises the post-training explanation as an account of why current incentives preserve or exacerbate some hallucinations [AR] (§3.3, “Error factors for base models”; §3.4, “Additional factors”; §4, “Post-training and hallucination”; §5, “Discussion and limitations”).

---

## 1. What the paper calls a hallucination

The paper uses **hallucination** for a plausible falsehood generated by a language model. It explicitly distinguishes this usage from human perceptual hallucination and from nonsensical output. In the formal model, plausible strings form a set \(\mathcal X=\mathcal E\cup\mathcal V\), partitioned into errors \(\mathcal E\) and valid strings \(\mathcal V\) [AP] (§1, “Introduction”; §5, “Plausibility and nonsense”).

Hallucinations are treated as an important special case of generation errors, not as the whole error category. The formal results apply to arbitrary designated sets of plausible errors; the hallucination application chooses \(\mathcal E\) to contain generations with one or more plausible falsehoods [AP] (§1, “Introduction”; §3.1, “Hallucination errors”).

The authors mention two common subclasses:

- **Intrinsic hallucinations** contradict the prompt, illustrated by models incorrectly counting the number of Ds in “DEEPSEEK” [AP] (§1, “Introduction”).
- **Extrinsic hallucinations** contradict the training data or external reality [AP] (§1, “Introduction”).

They also note an alternate definition—output not grounded in the training data or prompt. Under their deliberately favourable assumption that the training distribution contains only valid examples, a generated factual error cannot be grounded in factually correct training data, so the lower bound also covers that notion [AR] (§3.1, “Hallucination errors”).

### Motivating examples

When prompted for Adam Tauman Kalai's birthday only if it knew the answer, DeepSeek-V3 returned three different incorrect dates in three attempts [AP] (§1, “Introduction”; footnote 1). Asked for the title of Kalai's dissertation, three popular models each gave a different title and year; none generated the correct title or year [AP] (§1, Table 1).

The authors use these examples to distinguish arbitrary facts from representational limitations. An uncommon birthday may lack a learnable pattern or sufficient training evidence, whereas a letter-counting failure can reflect the model's representation and inference limitations [AR] (§1, “Introduction”; §3.3.1, “Arbitrary-fact hallucinations”; §3.3.2, “Poor models”).

---

## 2. The modern training pipeline in the paper

### Stage 1: pretraining

A base model \(\hat p\) is trained to approximate the distribution \(p\) of text in a corpus. The authors frame this as density estimation: learning a probability distribution over text, or over multimodal inputs when those are included [AP] (§3, “Pretraining Errors”).

The analysis assumes an error-free training distribution, \(p(\mathcal E)=0\), to establish a lower bound under favourable conditions. This is not a claim that real corpora are error-free. The authors repeatedly state that realistic corpora contain errors and half-truths and may therefore produce still higher error rates [AP] (§1, “Introduction”; §3.1, “The reduction without prompts”).

The paper does not reduce the phenomenon to next-token autocomplete or Transformer architecture. Its argument is about density estimation and applies broadly, including to reasoning and search-and-retrieval language models. Particular architectures can add further errors, but are not required for the reduction [AP] (§1, “Introduction”; §3, “Not merely autocomplete”).

### Stage 2: post-training

Post-training should shift the model from one trained like an autocomplete model to one that does not output confident falsehoods, except where appropriate, such as when asked to produce fiction. The paper's concern is that existing benchmarks and leaderboards reinforce certain types of hallucination, because binary scoring rewards a correct guess and gives abstentions no credit [AP] (§1.2, “Why hallucinations survive post-training”; §4, “Post-training and hallucination”).

The authors call this a **socio-technical** problem because changing an objective in isolation is insufficient: altered scoring must be adopted by the influential benchmarks and leaderboards that shape model development [AP] (§4, “Post-training and hallucination”).

---

## 3. The Is-It-Valid reduction

### Core intuition

Generating a valid response is at least as hard as recognising whether a proposed response is valid. Generation implicitly requires distinguishing valid candidates from plausible errors. The paper makes this relationship formal by showing how any base language model can be used as a classifier for the IIV binary-classification problem [AP] (§1.1, “Errors caused by pretraining”; §3, “Pretraining Errors”).

IIV is trained on a 50/50 mixture of:

1. valid examples sampled from the training distribution and labelled \(+\); and
2. uniformly selected plausible errors labelled \(-\) [AP] (§1.1, “Errors caused by pretraining”; §3.1, “The reduction without prompts”).

The base model induces a classifier by thresholding the probability it assigns to a candidate response. Intuitively, if the model assigns an error enough probability to cross the threshold, the induced classifier accepts that error as valid; if it assigns too little probability to a valid item, it rejects valid material [AP] (§3.1, “The reduction without prompts”).

### No-prompt setting

Without prompts, the base model is a distribution \(\hat p\) over plausible strings; the set of plausible strings is assumed finite for simplicity [AP] (§3.1, “The reduction without prompts”; footnote 4). Its generation error rate is

\[
\operatorname{err}=\hat p(\mathcal E).
\]

The induced IIV classifier accepts \(x\) when \(\hat p(x)>1/|\mathcal E|\). Corollary 1 gives

\[
\operatorname{err}\ge 2\operatorname{err}_{\mathrm{iiv}}
-\frac{|\mathcal V|}{|\mathcal E|}-\delta,
\]

where \(\delta=|\hat p(\mathcal A)-p(\mathcal A)|\) for the above-threshold set \(\mathcal A\) [AP] (§3.1, Corollary 1; formula transcribed).

The informal approximation in the introduction is therefore “(generative error rate) \(\gtrsim 2\cdot\) (IIV misclassification rate)” when the valid-to-error ratio and calibration term are small [AP] (§1.1, “Errors caused by pretraining”; §3.1, Corollary 1).

### Prompted setting

The general setting draws prompts \(c\) from a distribution \(\mu\), with valid response set \(\mathcal V_c\), error set \(\mathcal E_c\), training distribution \(p(r\mid c)\), and model \(\hat p(r\mid c)\). The error rate averages the probability of erroneous responses over prompts [AP] (§3.2, “The reduction with prompts”).

Training examples are therefore valid “dialogues” drawn from the same prompt distribution. The authors call this assumption unrealistic and note that even higher error rates may be expected when it fails [AP] (§3.2, “The reduction with prompts”).

Theorem 1 states, for a valid-only training distribution and any base model,

\[
\operatorname{err}\ge 2\operatorname{err}_{\mathrm{iiv}}
-\frac{\max_c|\mathcal V_c|}{\min_c|\mathcal E_c|}-\delta.
\]

Here the classifier accepts a prompt-response pair when \(\hat p(r\mid c)>1/\min_c|\mathcal E_c|\), and \(\delta\) compares model and training probability on the corresponding above-threshold set [AP] (§3.2, Theorem 1; formula transcribed).

The theorem is universal over base models under its setup, but its usefulness depends on the terms. A large IIV error gives a meaningful generation-error lower bound when the ratio of valid to erroneous responses and the calibration discrepancy are small [AR] (§3.1, Corollary 1; §3.2, Theorem 1).

### Calibration term

The paper's \(\delta\) is a threshold-specific calibration discrepancy, weaker than Expected Calibration Error. It can be estimated by comparing how often real training samples and synthetic model samples fall above the chosen probability threshold [AP] (§3.1, “Calibration”).

For the standard cross-entropy objective, the authors show that \(\delta\) is the magnitude of the loss derivative produced by rescaling above-threshold probabilities at scale one. If \(\delta\ne0\), a nearby rescaling reduces the loss; therefore a sufficiently expressive model near a local optimum should have small \(\delta\) [AR] (§3.1, “Calibration”).

A uniform distribution makes this particular \(\delta\) zero without any knowledge of the language, so \(\delta=0\) does not require \(\hat p=p\); Appendix D repeats the point that weak calibration of this kind is easy to have [AP] (§3.1, “Calibration”; Appendix D, “Computationally intractable hallucinations”).

### What “inevitable” does and does not mean

The paper's heading reads: **“Hallucinations are inevitable *only for base models*.”** [V] (§3.1). A non-hallucinating model could be built from a question-answer database and a calculator that answers a fixed set of questions and well-formed calculations and otherwise outputs IDK. The lower bound instead says that language models which do not err must not be calibrated; calibration, and hence errors, is a natural consequence of the standard cross-entropy objective [AR] (§3.1, “Hallucinations are inevitable only for base models”).

The authors point to GPT-4 calibration histograms from its technical report, before and after reinforcement learning, on multiple-choice queries; the caption states that the pretrained model is well calibrated, and the text contrasts base models, often found calibrated, with post-trained models, which may deviate from cross-entropy in favour of reinforcement learning. The figure is cited from the GPT-4 report, not a new experiment performed in this paper [AP] (§3.1, Figure 2).

---

## 4. Statistical error factors during pretraining

The reduction imports the familiar taxonomy of classification error into generation. The paper develops two factors in §3.3 and highlights three more in §3.4, one of which, computational hardness, gets a stylised formal treatment in Appendix D [AP] (§3.3, “Error factors for base models”; §3.4, “Additional factors”).

### 4.1 Arbitrary facts and epistemic uncertainty

An **arbitrary fact** has no succinct pattern from which the correct answer can be inferred. In the paper's stylised model, each prompt has one correct answer selected independently and uniformly from a response set, plus an IDK option; the training distribution sometimes supplies the answer and otherwise abstains [AP] (§3.3.1, Definition 1).

The birthday example fits this form: commonly discussed facts may occur many times, while another person's birthday may occur once or not at all. The formal model assumes one fixed way to write each fact, which makes the lower bound favourable; multiple surface forms may make the real problem harder [AP] (§3.3.1, “Arbitrary-fact hallucinations”).

A prompt is a **singleton** when it appears exactly once in \(N\) training examples with a non-IDK answer. The singleton rate \(\operatorname{sr}=|\mathcal S|/N\) estimates missing mass: the probability that a fresh draw from the training distribution is an answer (not IDK) to a prompt left unanswered in the sample [AP] (§3.3.1, Definition 2; Appendix B, Lemma 1).

This extends the Good–Turing intuition that outcomes seen once estimate the probability mass of outcomes not yet seen. The paper adapts the estimator so that abstentions are not counted as answered facts [AP] (§3.3.1, “Arbitrary-fact hallucinations”; Appendix B, “Arbitrary-facts analysis”).

Theorem 2 lower-bounds any algorithm's error in the arbitrary-facts model, with 99% probability, by approximately the singleton rate, minus finite-sample, response-set, and calibration terms:

\[
\operatorname{err}\ge \operatorname{sr}
-\frac{2}{\min_c|\mathcal E_c|}
-\frac{35+6\ln N}{\sqrt N}-\delta.
\]

It also states that an efficient algorithm outputting a calibrated \(\hat p\) (\(\delta=0\)) has, with 99% probability, error at most \(\operatorname{sr}-\operatorname{sr}/(\max_c|\mathcal E_c|+1)+13/\sqrt N\) [AP] (§3.3.1, Theorem 2; formulas transcribed).

It is a high-probability result in the stated random arbitrary-facts model, with explicit correction terms [AP] (§3.3.1, Theorem 2; Appendix B, proof of Theorem 2).

### 4.2 Poor models and representational mismatch

Misclassification can arise because the model family cannot represent the target boundary or because a sufficiently expressive family has been fitted poorly. The paper defines \(\mathrm{opt}(\mathcal G)\) as the minimum IIV classification error obtainable by a family of thresholded language-model classifiers [AP] (§3.3.2, “Poor models”).

Theorem 1 then yields a generation-error lower bound in terms of \(\mathrm{opt}(\mathcal G)\), along with the valid/error ratio and calibration terms. For pure multiple choice with one correct response among \(C\) choices, Theorem 3 removes the calibration term:

\[
\operatorname{err}\ge 2\left(1-\frac1C\right)\mathrm{opt}(\mathcal G).
\]

[AP] (§3.3.2, Theorem 3; formula transcribed).

The trigram illustration uses two prompts whose correct completions depend on a pronoun earlier than the two-word context. Any trigram model must generate an error with probability at least one half on the constructed distribution [AP] (§3.3.2, Corollary 2).

The DEEPSEEK letter-counting example is interpreted as a model limitation rather than an arbitrary fact. DeepSeek-R1 could reliably reason character by character where DeepSeek-V3 failed; tokenisation such as D/EEP/SEE/K makes the character-level property representationally awkward [AR] (§3.3.2, “Poor models”).

### 4.3 Computational hardness

Even a superhuman system running on a classical computer remains subject to computational complexity. The appendix constructs a secure-encryption example: without the secret key, an efficient system cannot distinguish correct decryptions from incorrect ones substantially better than chance [AP] (§3.4, “Additional factors”; Appendix D, “Computationally intractable hallucinations”).

Observation 2 applies Theorem 1 to that construction and lower-bounds erroneous decryptions for any model whose induced classifier does not break the cryptosystem. The example is explicitly stylised; the authors cite other work for more natural hard tasks [AP] (Appendix D, Observation 2).

### 4.4 Distribution shift

Errors can arise when the prompt distribution at use time differs from training. The paper uses “What's heavier, a pound of feathers or a pound of lead?” as a possible out-of-distribution question and notes that distribution shift may also contribute to the letter-counting example [AP] (§3.4, “Distribution shift”).

They treat distribution shift as a possible factor there, but because reasoning models count the letters correctly, they suggest poor models may be the greater factor [AR] (§3.4, “Distribution shift”).

### 4.5 Garbage in, garbage out

Real training corpora contain factual errors that base models may reproduce. The paper names this familiar mechanism **GIGO** and does not formalise it, because its statistical analogy to classification is direct [AP] (§3.4, “GIGO: Garbage in, Garbage out”).

Post-training can reduce some GIGO errors, including common misconceptions and conspiracy theories, but the next stage introduces its own incentive problem [AP] (§3.4, “GIGO: Garbage in, Garbage out”).

---

## 5. Why hallucinations survive post-training

### Binary grading rewards guessing

A binary grader assigns one point to a correct response and zero to incorrect answers and abstentions. If an uncertain model receives no credit for IDK, any answer with a non-zero probability of being marked correct has higher expected score than abstention [AP] (§1.2, “Why hallucinations survive post-training”; §4.1, “How evaluations reinforce hallucination”).

The authors' human analogy is exam-taking. Under zero-one scoring, students maximise expected marks by guessing; bluffs tend to be specific and overconfident. Models optimised against similar benchmarks are continually placed in that same test-taking regime [AR] (§1.2, “Why hallucinations survive post-training”).

Their concise diagnosis is: **“Put simply, most evaluations are not aligned.”** [V] (§1.2, “Why hallucinations survive post-training”).

### Observation 1

For prompt \(c\), let \(\mathcal A_c\) be plausible abstentions and let \(\rho_c\) represent the test-taker's uncertainty over binary graders. Observation 1 states that no abstention maximises expected score:

\[
\mathcal A_c\cap\arg\max_{r\in\mathcal R_c}
\mathbb E_{g_c\sim\rho_c}[g_c(r)]=\emptyset.
\]

[AP] (§4.1, Observation 1; formula transcribed).

The proof relies on the definition: every abstention always receives zero, while at least one non-abstaining response has positive probability of receiving one. The authors call the proof trivial [AP] (§4.1, “How evaluations reinforce hallucination”; Appendix E, proof of Observation 1).

### Why a specialised hallucination benchmark is insufficient

An aligned Model A that abstains when uncertain can lose to an otherwise similar Model B that always guesses, across the many accuracy and pass-rate evaluations that award abstention zero. A small number of hallucination-specific evaluations may therefore be outweighed by the larger portfolio of misaligned primary evaluations [AR] (§1.2, “Why hallucinations survive post-training”; §4.1, “How evaluations reinforce hallucination”).

The paper does not dismiss specialised hallucination evaluations. Its argument is that they cannot by themselves offset contrary incentives embedded in mainstream evaluations [AP] (§4.1, “How evaluations reinforce hallucination”).

### Meta-evaluation of influential benchmarks

The authors inspect ten evaluations used by influential leaderboards. Their summary table classifies GPQA, MMLU-Pro, IFEval, Omni-MATH, BBH, MATH Level 5, MuSR, SWE-bench, and HLE as binary with no IDK credit; WildBench is non-binary with only partial treatment of uncertainty [AP] (§4.1, Table 2; Appendix F, “Current grading of uncertain responses”).

For HELM's Capabilities leaderboard, four of five scenarios clearly give IDK no credit. The fifth, WildBench, may score an IDK response (3–4) lower than a “fair” response with factual errors or hallucinations (5–6), because an IDK does not help the user solve the problem in a meaningful way [AR] (Appendix F.1, “HELM Capabilities Benchmark”).

The Open LLM Leaderboard's six selected benchmarks use multiple-choice, exact-match, equivalence, or instruction-verification scoring that generally provides no abstention credit [AP] (Appendix F.2, “Open LLM Leaderboard”).

SWE-bench scores whether a patch passes tests, without distinguishing an incorrect patch from an uncertainty response. HLE's primary metric is binary accuracy; at the paper's writing, reported accuracy was below 30% [AP] (Appendix F.3, “SWE-bench and Humanity's Last Exam”).

HLE also reports calibration error, but the authors show that post-hoc confidence calibration is not itself a hallucination metric. A model could be always wrong and report zero confidence, or always correct and report zero confidence; those systems have opposite hallucination behaviour but calibration error alone does not express it [AR] (Appendix F.3, “SWE-bench and Humanity's Last Exam”).

Language-model judges create an additional risk: they can mark incorrect long answers as correct, even in mathematical domains, potentially adding reward for plausible bluffing [AP] (Appendix F, “Current grading of uncertain responses”).

---

## 6. Proposed mitigation: explicit confidence targets

The paper proposes that benchmark instructions state a confidence threshold \(t\) and the corresponding penalty for an incorrect answer:

> Answer only if you are $`>t`$ confident, since mistakes are penalized $`t/(1-t)`$ points, while correct answers receive 1 point, and an answer of “I don’t know” receives 0 points. [V] (§4.2, “Explicit confidence targets”)

Under this scoring rule, answering has higher expected value than IDK exactly when the probability of being correct exceeds \(t\). Example thresholds are \(t=0.5\), \(0.75\), and \(0.9\), which imply error penalties of 1, 2, and 9 respectively. Ordinary binary grading corresponds to \(t=0\) [AP] (§4.2, “Explicit confidence targets”).

The proposal has two distinguishing features:

1. **Put the target in the instructions.** The model should know the required confidence level, rather than being judged against an unstated error penalty [AP] (§4.2, “Explicit confidence targets”).
2. **Modify established evaluations.** Incorporate the targets into mainstream benchmarks such as SWE-bench, rather than limiting risk-sensitive scoring to bespoke hallucination evaluations [AP] (§4.2, “Explicit confidence targets”).

The authors call the desired response policy **behavioural calibration**: for each specified threshold, produce the most useful response whose correctness probability exceeds that threshold, otherwise abstain. This does not require emitting a numeric probability and can accommodate many valid phrasings [AP] (§4.2, “Explicit confidence targets”).

Behavioural calibration can be audited by comparing accuracy and error rates across explicit thresholds. The paper presents it as a potentially useful objective, not as a demonstrated property of current systems [AP] (§4.2, “Explicit confidence targets”).

The ideal threshold would reflect downstream harm, but that varies by application and user population. The authors prefer a transparent, possibly conventional threshold over an implicit and disputed penalty [AR] (§4.2, “Explicit confidence targets”).

---

## 7. Discussion, limits, and boundary conditions

### Plausibility versus nonsense

The main formalism restricts \(\mathcal X\) to plausible strings and therefore omits nonsense. Theorem 1 can be extended by adding a nonsense set \(\mathcal N\), defining error as probability mass on \(\mathcal N\cup\mathcal E\), and continuing to assume the training distribution is valid [AP] (§5, “Plausibility and nonsense”).

### Open-ended output

The examples emphasise single factual questions. Open-ended generations can be represented by treating any response containing one or more falsehoods as erroneous, but the authors acknowledge that a graded measure reflecting the number or severity of errors would be more natural [AP] (§5, “Open-ended generations”).

### Search and reasoning reduce risk but are not panaceas

Search and RAG can reduce hallucination, but Observation 1 applies to systems that use them: if retrieval does not yield a confident answer and scoring still rewards guessing, the incentive survives. Search may also not help with miscalculations such as the letter-counting example, or other intrinsic hallucinations [AP] (§5, “Search (and reasoning) are not panaceas”).

The section grants that a number of studies show search and RAG reduce hallucinations; its claim is that they are not panaceas [AP] (§5, “Search (and reasoning) are not panaceas”).

### Latent context

Some errors depend on context absent from the prompt-response pair. A question about “phones” may intend land lines while the model assumes cellphones. The paper's formal error definition cannot represent such hidden context and would need extension to address that aleatoric ambiguity [AP] (§5, “Latent context”).

### The false trichotomy

Correct, incorrect, and IDK do not capture degrees of error or uncertainty. The explicit-confidence proposal is pragmatic: even an incomplete trichotomy permits abstention, unlike the dominant false dichotomy [AR] (§5, “A false trichotomy”).

### Beyond literal IDK

Models can signal uncertainty by hedging, omitting doubtful detail, or asking a clarifying question. Numeric confidence can sometimes be useful but can also produce unnatural statements. The paper focuses on the top-level decision about what to say rather than solving the full pragmatics of uncertainty communication [AP] (§5, “Beyond IDK”).

## 8. Proof appendices and what each establishes

### Appendix A: proof of the main theorem

The proof partitions model and IIV errors into candidates above and below the probability threshold. Above threshold, each accepted error contributes at least twice as much to generation error as to IIV error. Below threshold, the missed-valid mass is bounded using the calibration discrepancy and the maximum number of valid responses relative to the minimum number of errors. Adding both parts gives Theorem 1 [AP] (Appendix A, “Proof of the main theorem”).

### Appendix B: arbitrary-facts analysis

The appendix first states a Good–Turing missing-mass concentration result, then adapts it to collapse all IDK responses and ignore abstentions when counting singletons. Lemma 1 bounds the difference between missing mass and singleton rate [AP] (Appendix B, Corollary 3; Lemma 1).

Lemma 2 states that, for any \(N\ge1\), \(\gamma\in(0,1]\), and any algorithm outputting \(\hat p\), with probability at least \(1-\gamma\), \(2\operatorname{err}_{\mathrm{iiv}}\ge\operatorname{sr}-6\ln(3N/\gamma)/\sqrt N\). The key independence step is that, for an unanswered prompt, the algorithm's output is independent of the randomly chosen correct answer [AP] (Appendix B, Lemma 2 and proof; formula transcribed).

Theorem 2 follows by combining Lemma 2 with Theorem 1. Its upper-bound construction memorises observed answers, matches the true abstention probability, and distributes answer probability uniformly for unanswered prompts; the proof verifies calibration for all thresholds in that construction [AP] (Appendix B, proof of Theorem 2).

### Appendix C: poor-model analysis

Theorem 4 strengthens the pure multiple-choice result by showing that some probability threshold yields the generation-error bound. Averaging over a uniformly random threshold links acceptance probability directly to model probability, allowing false-positive and false-negative IIV errors to be bounded by generation error [AP] (Appendix C, Theorem 4 and proof).

The trigram corollary follows because no thresholded trigram classifier can distinguish the constructed pair of prompts, fixing its IIV error at one half [AP] (Appendix C, proof of Corollary 2).

### Appendix D: computational hardness

The secure-encryption construction maps correct prompt-decryption pairs to valid examples and random mismatches to errors. If the induced classifier cannot break encryption, Theorem 1 forces a high erroneous-decryption rate for a calibrated model [AP] (Appendix D, Definition 3; Observation 2).

### Appendix E: post-training analysis

The proof of Observation 1 shows that all abstentions score zero under every binary grader while some non-abstaining response has positive expected score. Therefore abstention cannot be optimal [AP] (Appendix E, proof of Observation 1).

### Appendix F: current grading of uncertain responses

The appendix documents how HELM Capabilities, the Open LLM Leaderboard, SWE-bench, and HLE treat uncertainty. It supplies the benchmark-level support for Table 2 and qualifies edge cases such as BBQ, which explicitly includes unknown answers in a safety scenario, and WildBench, which uses a graded rubric [AP] (Appendix F.1–F.3).

## 10. Connections the authors make in the text

The converted tape drops author names from in-text citations (pandoc renders them as blanks, e.g. “The most closely related theoretical work is by , which…”), so the cited works below are described as the paper frames them, not by name.

- The authors state that, to their knowledge, their reduction from supervised learning (binary classification) to unsupervised learning (density estimation or self-supervised learning) is novel, while reduction between learning problems is a well-established technique for showing one problem is at least as hard as another [AP] (§2, “Related work”).
- Surveys and studies of hallucination's causes cite factors including model overconfidence, decoding randomness, snowballing effects, long-tailed training samples, misleading alignment training, spurious correlations, exposure bias, the reversal curse, and context hijacking [BT] (§2).
- The most closely related theoretical work connected Good–Turing missing-mass estimates to hallucinations and is, the authors show, a special case of their reduction; it did not address uncertainty expressions such as IDK, connections to supervised learning, post-training, or prompts. An earlier version of this paper presented a related theorem that omitted prompts and abstentions [BT] (§2; §1.1; §3.3.1).
- Other theoretical studies formalise a trade-off between consistency (avoiding invalid outputs) and breadth: for broad classes of languages, a model that generalises beyond its training data either hallucinates or suffers mode collapse [BT] (§2).
- RLHF, RLAIF and DPO have been shown to reduce hallucinations, including conspiracy theories and common misconceptions; simple fine-tuning on novel information can initially decrease hallucination rates, only for them to increase later [BT] (§2).
- The authors report that relatively little work has examined barriers to adopting hallucination benchmarks [AP] (§2). They cite the 2025 AI Index report’s observation that these benchmarks “have struggled to gain traction within the AI community.” [V] (§2).

## 12. Citation and source-integrity notes

- **Citation style:** `(§ N, "Section name")`; appendices use `(Appendix A–F, "Heading")`. These anchors follow the official submission and survive deterministic TeX conversion. Page citations are intentionally not used because the clean TeX conversion does not preserve page boundaries.
- **Complete-source coverage:** The full official TeX body, all six appendices, footnotes, and the complete 94-entry BBL bibliography were read. The official 36-page PDF (arXiv:2509.04664v1) confirms the page count, the six appendices, the 94 bibliography entries and both figures. It also shows a loss in the tape: Table 1's footnote (PDF footnote 3, which gives the access date, access route and model version for each dissertation-title query and states that none of the models searched the Web) and the two author notes are absent, so the tape's footnotes 3–8 are the PDF's footnotes 4–9. Footnote numbers cited in this reference follow the tape (footnote 4 here is the PDF's footnote 5).
- **Conversion caveat:** The converted tape contains six appendices, eight footnotes, and 94 bibliography entries, but many in-text citation identities are missing and some bibliography titles are incomplete (for example, the GPT-4 technical report appears as “-4 Technical Report” and the HELM Capabilities blog entry has no title). Section coverage and bibliography-entry counts do not establish citation-level completeness; resolving those identities needs the original TeX/BBL or PDF.
- **Figures:** Figure 1 illustrates the IIV classification regimes. Figure 2 reproduces GPT-4 calibration histograms from the GPT-4 technical report; it is not a new experiment run by these authors.
- **Evidence markers:** `[V]` marks exact source language in quotation marks; formulas re-typeset from the source's LaTeX are marked `[AP]` with “formula transcribed”, because the notation is not character-exact; `[BT]` marks a claim the authors take from cited work; `[AP]` marks a paraphrase of the authors' text; `[AR]` marks the authors' reasoning or an inference they make from their framework. Unmarked list items immediately under a marked lead sentence inherit that sentence's anchor.
- **Attribution boundary:** Claims the paper takes from other studies remain claims reported by these authors unless the underlying work is independently audited. This reference does not import facts from the bibliography merely because they are cited there.
- **Model boundary:** The formal lower bounds concern base models under specified distributional and calibration assumptions. They do not prove that every possible AI system must hallucinate.
- **Causal boundary:** The post-training section establishes that binary scoring rewards guessing and documents its prevalence in selected influential evaluations. It does not experimentally estimate how much of any named deployed model's hallucination rate was caused by those evaluations.
- **Bibliography order:** The converted source tape places the bibliography after the appendices, matching the canonical working conversion assembled from the official TeX and BBL files.
